01 / About

Children first.
Curiosity always.

I am a researcher dedicated to making children’s digital storytelling more beneficial for their social and emotional development and their academic learning, particularly in STEM.

Screens are here to stay. As researchers, creators, and caregivers, we have a responsibility to make time spent on screens as emotionally and academically beneficial as possible.

I am a Ph.D. student in Education at the University of California, Irvine, working with Dr. Mark Warschauer and Dr. Andres Bustamante. My research focuses on the power of storytelling within the Latinx community to engage young Latinx learners in STEM subjects and build fundamental STEM skills.

My work includes analyzing nine co-design sessions with Latine families to guide the development of bilingual ebooks.

03 / Research & Projects

Storytelling.

Collaborative work with families, children’s media, and the stories that support learning.

ACCESS NSF-supported research

ACCESS
STEM ebooks

I am working on an NSF grant focused on collaborative-based design with the Latine community to create bilingual STEM ebooks.

I’ve been guiding graduate students in leading co-design sessions with Latine families in Santa Ana to understand the books and stories that reflect their needs and interests. This research draws on funds of knowledge and storytelling traditions to support STEM engagement and early STEM skills for young Latine learners.

  • Co-design with families
  • Bilingual ebooks
  • Early STEM learning

ACCESS

AI Literacy

A colleague and I saw our co-design sessions as an opportunity to introduce our Latine family partners to the beginnings of AI literacy. Families used ChatGPT to create concept art for the ebooks while learning about AI.

The concept art, together with families’ likes, dislikes, and critiques, helps guide Ernesto, our artist, in drawing the ebooks. The AI-generated images serve as concepts for the professional illustrations.

Public writing

Bluey Blog Post

This article explores how Bluey models the power of imaginative play to support children’s creativity, emotional development, and family connection.

Drawing on developmental research, it highlights how everyday moments—like playing in the rain or pretending to be doctors—can become rich learning experiences for children and parents alike.

Storytelling with Latine Families

My research would not be possible without the creativity and hard work of the many families I collaborate with. This work also carries their powerful voices and stories. Their experiences with AI-generated concept art opened conversations about critical use, safety, and bias.

A childhood memory, brought back to life

One mother had no pictures of her childhood in El Salvador. Missing that time in her life, she wanted to recreate a memory. When she saw the AI-generated image, she began to cry: it showed a small version of herself caked in mud, the only girl in the street playing soccer. Her family couldn’t afford shoes, but she told herself she could run faster without them. The image brought her joy, while the process also introduced conversations about how AI works, critical use, bias, and safety.

Super Y: a superhero for children of all abilities

Super Y is a superhero who fights for children of all abilities to feel welcome, safe, and loved, in environments that avoid over- or understimulation.

Recognizing bias in generative AI

When asked to create “3 Latino cows,” the generated image prompted a mother to comment, “Luce Como Cholos” (“They look like chicano gangsters”). Her response highlighted stereotypes in the output. The example became an opportunity to discuss AI literacy, including safety, critical use, and awareness of bias. These conversations help family partners evaluate and question the representations generative AI produces.

04 / Podcasts

Conversations
through the screen.

Children’s media, representation, development, and the stories we watch together.

Gotta Be Done · Bluey

Powerful Children’s Media

My Bluey blog writing team, including Dr. Molly Scout and Ph.D. student Doug Piper, was invited onto the Bluey podcast Gotta Be Done. We had a fabulous discussion with Kate McMahon and Mary Bolling about the powerful work happening on Bluey. Children’s development is important, and with so much time on screens, they should be watching shows made with children’s best interests in mind. We discuss why Bluey is the phenomenon that it is, how it incorporates child development research and classical music, and how it illustrates parenting in a unique way.

Listen on Spotify

She-Ra and the Princesses of Power

Powerful Princesses

We discuss She-Ra and the Princesses of Power, the reboot of the 1980s show. While the original show was created to sell toys, this adaptation focuses on great stories, representation of underrepresented groups, and a world free of toxic masculinity. We explore the good and bad representation in the show and how watching it might affect younger viewers.

Watch the episode

Indie animation & storytelling

Magical Girl

Discussing I Don’t Want to Be a Magical Girl, an animatic pilot on YouTube, we take a deep dive into the 11-minute pilot, the reimagined animation industry, and the ways indie animation is finding new and creative routes for more unique stories.

Watch the episode

Social & emotional learning

Heartstopper

We discuss the social and emotional learning viewers can do while watching Heartstopper. The show represents romantic and platonic connections with good communication. Its teenagers are not always expert communicators, but they learn from those around them to build positive relationships grounded in trust and communication.

View the episode on Patreon

With Theo Ho · Coming soon

Through the Screen

A podcast with Theo Ho about parenting in the digital age and ways parents can use media to connect with their children and support learning. Our first episode is about Bluey; after that, we plan to discuss episodes of Avatar: The Last Airbender, which I consider one of the best pieces of media geared toward children.

05 / Interests

The stories, stitches,
and stages in between.

Children’s TV Media

I work in children’s media because it is something I am truly passionate about. Media affects us all, but young children are highly susceptible to its messages. In a world where we are bombarded by new media, it can be hard to choose as a parent. If you ever want recommendations, I’m happy to provide them. I also tell parents about Common Sense Media, which rates media for children and offers lots of parent guides.
